title: Geometric Origin of the Hubble Flow: Reconciling Planck and SH0ES Boundaries via the 3.998D Fractional Manifold
content: The Hubble tension represents two measurements of the same cosmic expansion rate, where local distance-ladder yields ~ 73 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, while Planck’s CMB analyses results in a lower value of ~ 67.4 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. Herein, we show that this discrepancy may be a geometric effect within a 3.998D Manifold defining Space. We build on the framework’s prior successes in reproducing galactic rotation curves, galaxy cluster dynamics, and the CMB acoustic peaks using a handful of derived primitive constants recycled across scales. In particular, we demonstrate that a single density-dependent saturation mechanism and a universal vacuum friction, arising from a spectral dimension of 3.998, simultaneously account for both the local excess and the apparent cosmic acceleration. The framework shows that photon propagation is governed by a path integral incorporating entropic leakage modulated by the saturation function. The leakage is mathematically shown to vanish locally, preserving General Relativity (GR) and Newtonian physics, recovering ~ 72.64 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. This value steadily diverges in deep voids, producing ~ 67.4 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ lower value from the cumulative leakage effects along the photon path. The Pantheon+ catalogue is examined, revealing a near statistical parity with ΛCDM (with reduced χ² ~ 0.605 against ΛCDM’s ~ 0.548), while remaining competitive in the local horizon (~0.793 against ΛCDM’s ~0.851). Further validation against cosmic chronometers is performed, confirming structural stability across the light cone, and a prior-free quasar flux analysis at z > 2, hints at systematic drifts introduced by ΛCDM-preconditioned templates. Notably, these results are achieved across all observable scales using the framework’s fixed, scale-independent geometric constants, derived once from the 4-simplex topology and a fixed dimensional deficit of 0.002, with no retuning or sector-specific adjustments to accommodate different observables. The convergence of these outputs against the backdrop of observational data suggests the need for a re-evaluation of whether any single model should serve as the exclusive interpretive lens through which cosmological data are examined.
